hops.title: A one-celled umbrella showed what the nucleus does
hops.text: In the 1930s, biologist Joachim Hämmerling studied Acetabularia, a single-celled alga shaped like a tiny green umbrella. It grows a few centimeters tall, with its lone nucleus down in the root-like foot. When Hämmerling joined the stalk of one species to the foot of another, the first caps looked like the stalk's species or a mix of both. The last caps matched the species whose foot held the nucleus.

hops.afterHeading: Explain: the parts work as a team
hops.title: Skunk cabbage uses its mitochondria to melt snow
hops.text: Skunk cabbage blooms in late winter, even with snow on the ground. Its flower cells speed up cellular respiration in their mitochondria, releasing stored food energy as heat that can melt snow. In one study, the insides of the flower spikes stayed 15 to 35 degrees Celsius warmer than the air, even below freezing. For at least 14 days they used oxygen about as fast as warm-blooded animals their size.

hops.title: The cells in the middle of your eye's lens have no nucleus
hops.text: You might think every living cell in your body needs a nucleus and mitochondria to do its job. Yet you are reading this sentence partly through cells in the center of your lens that threw both away. These cells pack themselves with clear proteins, then dismantle their own nucleus, ER and mitochondria. Left in place, those parts could scatter light, and removing them helps keep the lens clear.

audio.title: Three cells that break the textbook picture
audio.transcript:
When you picture a cell from a textbook, you probably see a neat little dot, way too small to spot without a microscope, holding one tidy set of parts. Real cells are much wilder than that. Here are three true stories where cell parts do the unexpected.

First, meet a cell you do not even need a microscope to see. It is a green alga called Acetabularia. It looks like a tiny green umbrella, with a root-like foot, a long stalk, and a little cap on top. It can grow a few centimeters tall, and the whole thing is still just one single cell, with one single nucleus tucked way down in its foot. Back in the nineteen thirties, a biologist named Joachim Hämmerling noticed that two species of Acetabularia grew differently shaped caps. So he did a tiny bit of cell surgery. He swapped the stalks, so each foot carried the other species' stalk. Then he waited to see what kind of new cap would grow. At first, a new cap could look like the stalk's species, or like a mix of both. But the later caps matched the species that owned the foot with the nucleus. Even from centimeters away, that lone nucleus held the instructions for what the cell should build.

Now jump from a giant alga right into your own face. You might figure that every working cell in your body needs to keep its nucleus and mitochondria. After all, the nucleus holds the instructions and mitochondria release energy from food. Yet right now, light is passing into your eyes through living cells that broke down both of them as they grew up. Inside the clear lens of your eye, young cells start out with the usual team of parts. Using instructions from their nucleus, they pack themselves full of clear proteins. Once that building job is finished, the cells in the middle of the lens break down and clear away their own nucleus, their E R, and their mitochondria. Why? Left in place, organelles could scatter light, so those cells clear them out. It helps keep your lens clear enough to read this.

Finally, head outdoors at the end of winter. In wet woods and swamps in eastern North America, skunk cabbage often blooms before spring arrives, sometimes with snow still on the ground. Its flower cells rev up cellular respiration in their mitochondria, taking in oxygen and breaking down stored food to release heat. In one study, the insides of eastern skunk cabbage flower spikes stayed fifteen to thirty-five degrees Celsius warmer than the air, even when the air was well below freezing. For at least two weeks, they used oxygen about as fast as warm-blooded animals of similar size. That heat can melt nearby snow. A plant with a built-in space heater, powered by mitochondria.

One giant umbrella cell run from its foot, eye cells that clear out their own parts, and a snow-melting flower powered by mitochondria. Which parts a cell keeps, and how it uses them, depends on the job it does.
